review_text: Justin's lectures and notes are comprehensive. Tips: Make use of TA office hours and visit Justin's office for any questions or clarifications. Attend lectures, especially if you prefer a hands-on approach over simply reading latex notes. review_text: In my opinion, Herman is a vastly underrated professor. He has three midterms and a final, and each is worth about 15-18% of your grade. He posts a 20-30 page long practice test about a week before each exam, thats filled with practice questions that are formatted and cover similar content as the corresponding exam. Basically, if you do the whole practice test and understand everything within it, you are set for the actual exam. He also posts worksheets in the form of optional homework that are good practice for exams. In terms of exam grading, he and his TA's are generally pretty generous with the grading, and I often found myself getting a higher grade than I expected. In terms of lectures, he doesnt allow electronics, which didnt really affect me as I dont use electronics in any of my classes, but he tends to be a pretty good lecturer. He covers the material at a good pace, and is very open to questions about the content. Hes also pretty funny and seems to care about his students imo. He and his TAs have plenty of office hours, and when he didnt have time to cover certain material in class, he went out of his way to make videos about it rather than direct us to the textbook to learn it ourselves, he also gave everyone three pieces of candy for halloween. He does incentivise people to come to lecture and discussion by having "surprise" graded worksheets that are cumulatively worth about 10% of the grade, so if you go to lecture and discussion, you basically get a free 10% of your grade as the worksheets are graded on completion. He also has participation points that are worth 3% of your grade where you basically have to participate a few times over the sem, so another easy 3%. As for projects, none of them were super hard, I think the longest one took me like 3 hours, he released the grades for the first two fairly quickly but waited till the end of the sem for the rest of them. He gives long instructions for the projects which have a lot of helpful details and as long as you follow that and style your code correctly you should be fine, he also gave extra credit for some of them if you finish them before the deadline. Basically, Herman is a good lecturer who cares about his students and gives ample resources and grade boosters so you can get a good grade in the class, just make sure to attend lectures and discussions and you should do fine.

label_rationale: The course is exam-heavy, but grading and resources are generous; project grades are delayed.

review_text: The concepts in this class definitely have the potential to be cool and engaging, but the way he teaches is quite disorganized and detailed in the wrong places. You learn a bunch of vocab words in every lecture that gets mentioned once and never reiterated, but he keeps moving forward so if you don't remember one word you're screwed. Even if you read the textbook, the terminology it uses is sometimes different than the terminology he uses in class. He also moves really fast and all his slides have a lot of words, so it feels impossible to take notes and if you get lost, you're not going to pick up anything for the rest of the class. He also frequently makes mistakes in his lectures or slides and has to double back on himself during class which makes knowing what is the "correct" information rather difficult. As for the assignments, they take a long time, and he lied about having only 6 assignments (we had 7). The instructions for almost every assignment were constantly changed, even up to a few days before the due date. There's almost always some type of unforeseen issue with it that several people have to address before it gets announced to the rest of the class. The exams are multiple choice which takes some stress off, but the difficulty really isn't any better, especially when you see that one question is worth 9% of your whole exam grade. The one exam on logic is literally just 250 + genuine logic. If you have your cheat sheet of definitions you don't have to go to class to get a good score if your logical reasoning abilities are strong. On the other hand, if they're not but you studied a lot, you might not do so well. The exams themselves often contain a few poorly worded questions that leave it up for interpretation, and when you ask for clarification from the TAs, they also interpret it differently than how he intended and you get the question wrong. The exams could be better structured, but at least there's a curve on it. Two stars just because there's a curve, the textbook he recommends is well written/easy to understand, and these two together + self studying make this class passable.

review_text: Interestingly, this professor was substituted into teaching this class at the last minute; I had registered for Anurag Dey just to walk in on the first day and instead see this dripped out mess of a man. Anyways, his first crime was making the first homework due after the schedule adjustment period ended. As someone who doesn't touch homework until the day it was due, I would have probably dropped the class if I had known it would be like that. Consistently, the homework had very conceptual questions, and at least one proof each. Eventually I wised up and realized that these are all well explained proofs and that I could just go to MathStackExchange or https://statproofbook.github.io and copy from there. These proofs were never on the exams except for one time we were asked to derive the pmf of a negative hypergeometric distribution based on our knowledge of negative binomial and hypergeometric. That was criminal. The quizzes were easy except for the two or three times that they were not. My TA was very unorganized (had an excused absence and turned a HW in one day late by emailing him, it took him a long time to reply). Also, at least this semester, all the grades were on Gradescope and did not account for the curves and weighting, so you had to calculate your actual grade by hand; somewhat annoying. After the first midterm, he got coerced (bullied?) into having a curve, giving extra credit opportunities on the HW, and giving a formula sheet for the second midterm, along with posting more helpful practice problems. The EC questions were always ridiculously difficult, so I'm not sure how many people benefitted from this. At least for the final, I thought the practice problems were reflective of what was on the exam, and instead of a formula sheet, we were allowed to bring a cheat sheet with whatever we wanted on it. Despite the number of times I cried over the class (mostly the homework), I also literally jumped for joy when I would get a 100% on the homework. This class had me going through it. Not to mention that his lectures are just abysmal, see below re bad handwriting, tangents, not to mention the weeks we spent wondering what symbol he was drawing and talking about ("co-see"). Finally, a book I was reading during one of Zheng's lectures for my English class said something about xi and the mystery was solved. Lecture was best spent taking notes from the "class text", the draft of notes by two other UMD stats professors, while occasionally looking up to see what he was talking about. He has a way of explaining easy concepts in the worst way possible. Instead of saying "turn right", he would say "turn left three times". Also, he doesn't post a link to the class text anywhere, so you have to hope you can look it up or a friend sends it to you. Just poorly organized, but it's his first semester, so maybe he'll lock in soon like he does on his fits.
evidence_snippet: homework had very conceptual questions
label_rationale: Homework is demanding, lectures are ineffective, and the course is poorly organized.

review_text: This class is flipped lecture which means we watch the lecture videos on our own, and go into class to ask questions for one of the classes for the week. The other class for the week (not listed on testudo as a class/discussion time) is a workshop where we do an assignment on that week's lecture content. The content of the course is ok. It's all pertinent to the subject, and is realistic for students to learn at this level. However, the logistics for this class and it's assignments were some of the worst I've ever taken at CS at Maryland. This professor does not teach, and it feels like he does not care about this class at all. He was not present at the midterm to answer questions, and when we asked the TA's questions at the midterm, they said "Let me ask the Professor" and then the professor would not respond, so the TA's did their best in answering our questions for the midterm. Every homework assignment released with bugs, meaning if you wanted to start the homework early, you'd have to post on piazza about the bug, wait for the TA's to fix it, and then start again. Every homework assignment had extremally vague instructions and grading criteria spawning many questions on the piazza. These questions were often answered by complete non answers, or "you should know this". Might I add that the in person question sessions were not recorded, so if you could not remember what a TA/Professor said during class, there was no way to get that answer. So, if they answered a piazza question in class, you're just left hoping another student will answer it for you. In completing the homeworks, many of the lecture videos were wholly unhelpful as well. The videos are not substantial enough to teach the content to a level needed to complete the homeworks in my opinion. To complete them, I would go back to reference the lecture videos, only to realize he spent maybe a sentence or two on implementation details we need for the homework, and the rest of the video introing why this technique is important in history, or why it fell out of favor. All in all, the class felt lazy, sloppy, and an absolute nuisance to complete assignments. I strongly recommend against taking CMSC470 with this professor.

The biggest change Shankar could've done is go over hints for the projects in the lecture, though this was mostly the job of the discussion section and the TAs. Other changes Shankar could've made were to make his slides less vague and provide more detailed practice exam solutions. 412 is hard because doing the GeekOS projects take too long, leaving students without much time for other classes and to understand other aspects of Operating Systems not implemented in GeekOS. GeekOS is designed by a UMD graduate, Jeffrey Hollingsworth, Neil Spring, etc. If one accounts for the fact that this project was given to everyone who took CMSC 412, one would realize that this pain is not the fault of the Shankar but the curriculum of the course. review_text: I took this class in Spring 2021. Typically, while most people say that your 451 grade with Kruskal is the same as your 351 grade with Kruskal, I feel as though your 451 grade may be lower. If you choose to take this class with Kruskal, be sure you know what you're doing... Pros: + The ridiculously long pre lecture videos from 351 are gone. The professor actually teaches new content during lecture time, making lectures highly informative. + He repeats most NP assignments from 351, so you can reuse your work + Professor is very chill regarding deadlines. Often, he would extend a homework deadline by a few dates simply because someone asked nicely. Our midterm deadline was actually moved by 2 weeks. Cons: - The quizzes from 351 that helped gauge your progress are (mostly) gone. We had a few at the beginning of the semester but they stopped afterwards - There are no written solutions given for any homework assignment (not just NP). This is especially detrimental when exams are often based off of homework assignments. While there are review sessions that go over homework assignments, they lack the formal rigor that a written solution would have. Also, there is no guarantee that the every problem is covered in these sessions. It is especially baffling that we do not have solution keys when this was done so often back in 351. - The live lectures are often very free-flowing and not directed without the slide set. This can make it difficult to determine what to take notes on. - No review material is given for either the midterm or final. The homework assignments do not make up for this. As a result, it is very easy to lose lots of points of exam questions where you may actually understand the concepts at hand. Again, exam review material is something that was easily made for 351, so I am shocked that they couldn't apply the same processes here to make it.
evidence_snippet: exams are often based off homework assignments

So you should work on them well before the exam so you can get assistance from him or the TA's if you're stuck. review_text: Now, Neil is a great guy and a somewhat competent teacher. He writes it very colloquially which is nice, but sometimes he uses really obnoxiously large, outmoded words (draconian, pathological etc.). This class is more demanding than any other I have ever taken, and it's in no small part because of the disparity in intelligence of the individuals who take it. review_text: I would give ZERO stars if I would. This is both the hardest and worst course that I've ever had the displeasure of taking at UMD. I enrolled in this class because I thought that Operating Systems is a fundamental and useful skill to learn, even if difficult, but found out that the administration of this class makes this 10x more harder for literally no reason. There are so many things wrong with this course that I wouldn't recommend ANYONE taking it because it's not worth it. First of all, others seemed to like the professor's lecturing ability, but I did not. He goes on tangents all the time and is very unclear in his statements that it is impossible to focus. The slides are comprehensive, but are taken straight from the textbook so that isn't really a credit to the professor. The projects and exams though, that is a different hell. Let's talk projects. Each one is incredibly difficult, and the instructions are HORRIBLE. There is really no valid reason why there should be a spec, slides, and FAQ for EVERY SINGLE PROJECT. The spec is awfully written and flat out wrong about things, the project slides are vague and also have incorrect information. The FAQs don't answer certain questions with any new information, and the fact that an FAQ is even needed for a project means that the instructions are poorly written. And to make things worse, even the spec, slides, and FAQ are sometimes not enough. On a related note, administration for this course was TRULY TERRIBLE. Questions on Piazza were just left unanswered even though there were many people with the same question; the TAs just didn't answer and weren't active. I'm pretty sure they were also left in the dark about logistics in the class, because it was near the end of the semester and we STILL did not have breakdowns of grading. That part of the course website was just never filled out. And one of our pop quizzes, which we only had 10 minutes to do and had a very poor average, was worth almost an entire project grade. That is completely ridiculous and shows how little the professor cares about administration for this class. For exams, we didn't get any review material, no study guide or previous exams, zip, zilch, nada. Just "look at the slides" which are hundreds if not thousands of slides so it's impossible to study everything on it. In addition, for our final, the professor was very unaccommodating to concerns over the Omicron variant, and refused to move the final online despite multiple CS classes shifting online, and almost the entire class requesting this change. No reasoning was given, of course. Lastly, our final exam, which is worth a quarter of our final grade, was put on the grade server, and we never even got it back to see what we got wrong, let alone a regrade request. It was simply put on Testudo. This fact may change since this review is posted, but nevertheless it is inexcusable to have these final grades submitted without students seeing the reason, especially when this resource is easily available via Gradescope. I get that Operating Systems is a hard concept, but like I said, the administration made this course needlessly more difficult. I am sure that most other people in the class agree with me regarding the majority of the points that I raised here, and there are probably more points that I didn't mention. These points are definitely fixable (having clear grading, clear project descriptions, enforcing Piazza answering, giving us study material) and should definitely be addressed the next time this course is taken. I find that unlikely to happen though, so I do not recommend this course to anyone until then. You're better off looking at the slides or textbook on your own.
evidence_snippet: Each one is incredibly difficult...instructions are HORRIBLE
label_rationale: Extremely difficult projects and exams are compounded by unclear instructions and poor administration.

review_text: As a student, I was incredibly interested in the possibility of taking an artificial intelligence course at UMD. However the biggest thing that was a let down was the way the course was instructed and the instructors themselves. Max is most definitely incredibly knowledged about the subject, and seems to have a passion for AI itself. However, the course was by far the worst organized 400 level course I have taken at UMD, and that's coming from a university with many "below average" professors in the computer science department. First and foremost, no enforcement of the material was given throughout the year. The course "material" was directly copied and ripped off from CS188, Berkeley's Intro to AI course. The slides, were directly copied as well. As a student, I found it much more effective to visit Berkeley's website and learn from their instructors instead. Signing up for this course would be a waste of your tuition when you can simply learn the material yourself using the CS188 website. Even the midterm itself was given with a low effort on the instructors part. The midterm was given online in class. Almost all students found the midterm to be impossible to complete in the given time, and this resulted in a low average for the exam. Instructors had to remove an entire section of the midterm after grading to better curve the results, which meant that students spent time on that section for no reason. There were 3 total homeworks given in the class. Homeworks 2 and 3 provided more of a learning experience and had more applicability to the course material in comparison to anything else we'd ever learned in class. Homework 3 was building an image classifier using a nueral network which ended up being the most helpful and interesting project done in the class. This project was done using PyTorch, however Max provided absolutely no guidance on how to start with PyTorch leading students to self learn the material before being able to start the homework itself. The final project was a group project, but yet again students were misinformed of the requirements. We were orginally told to complete a short report on our project, but a week before the deadline, this was changed to a 3-5 page report. Moreover, the grading procedure of the final project was not given until a week before the deadline. The lack of communication and help with both the homeworks and the final project speaks to how poorly the class was run. Overall, it seems that some individuals are not meant to teach no matter how knowledgable they are in the material, and Max is one of them.

label_rationale: Students self-learned project tools while facing impossible exams and shifting project requirements.

There are times where an actual new or interesting concept will be introduced in lecture but more often than not you will walk away wondering what you actually learned in that 50 minute period. As for coursework the bulk of the grade comes from 4 exams, one of which is dropped. Most of them are relatively easy if you have any programming experience at all but there's a few questions that are about very specific techniques in python. The 3 homeworks throughout the semester are sort of the projects you would expect of a programming course which aside from the final project are the most time consuming. But even then if you have any programming experience at all you could finish one in 1 or 2 hours and you have unlimited attempts so you can just keep debugging and resubmitting until you check all the boxes which is nice. Considering this is the main programming course of the info sci major, I can't say this course had the rigor I expected. Maybe that sounds great to some of you but if you're expecting a programming course that has any difficulty then this is not it. Even the final project felt like a softball and the hardest part was getting your group members to commit and push to github. Most of the other assignments are just you explaining certain concepts in your own words and then provide working examples yourself which I find would be unhelpful to anyone learning python for the first time. And everyone else talking about the grading is not making it up. I kid you not, I waited until a few days before final grades were due and I got everything graded all at once in the span of an hour. So don't expect to get any grades back throughout the semester or know what your grade is at all. Overall the course structure felt really unorganized and most of the assignments weren't all that helpful aside from the homework's and group project. I'd recommend him if you have a decent understanding of python so you can just coast through the class without too much concern because if you are trying to learn python from this course, you're in for a rough time.

review_text: Before I get into my review, I should note that the C+ is pretty much entirely on me. I should have taken the course more seriously, especially for the first midterm, and I got burned for not doing so. At least I passed. With that said, this class did not work for me whatsoever. It's not because the class is hard, though it absolutely is, and I'd argue it should be. I just don't think it's for the right reasons. For instance, the lecture/exam half of the course is almost entirely disjoint from the GeekOS project half of the course, and it really feels like a 5/6 credit course sometimes. Being good at the lecture content will not help you whatsoever with GeekOS, and vice versa. This seems to be a 412-wide issue. Regarding the lecture content, I don't think Pete is a very good lecturer. It's sort of what the other reviewers this semester so far have pointed out. I wouldn't quite agree with the tin can rattling mentality, but he certainly doesn't practice his presentations, and he brings absolutely no energy to the class. Another reviewer pointed out the ChatGPT image, which he said he would fix and never did, but there was another instance where he took a TRIO slide set from the internet, didn't review it at all beforehand, and tried going through it in a rather miserable showing. There's very little transformation of his slide content in his lectures, as all he does is take his laser pointer and point to things he wants to emphasize on one of the projectors in the room. The slides themselves are rather poor summaries of OSTEP, which he follows very closely. That's just lectures themselves. The assignments he gives aren't much better in my opinion. He assigns weekly Gradescope reading homeworks which are worth 1% of the grade each. I honestly almost wish he would give more traditional homeworks instead. Some of the questions are horribly ambiguous, there's no room to state any assumptions, there are some questions where it feels like even with both the slides and OSTEP you can't really answer well, they ultimately lack engagement, and they are nowhere near comprehensive enough to actually prepare for the exams imo. Regarding exams, exam 1 was insane with the short answer questions of random topics from the slides being worth so much of the grade, while exams 2 and 3, especially 3, were relatively more chill. These certainly weren't my strongsuit, as I'm horrible with memorizing topics which I haven't worked directly with in some meaningful way, and I'm rather terrible at studying. I didn't like them, but they were fine I guess. One question I would like to address is the barber shop semaphore problem in exam 2. Not only were the semantics poorly defined, as the professor admitted, but in my experience, semaphore programming isn't just something just I get right away. I haven't worked with them before, as I haven't had any need to. They really weren't gone over well in class, nor were the gradescope assignments enough to really nail it in. He didn't give any other practice problem on them besides the baboon problem from a reading homework. I realize this is just one specific example, but it's emblematic of my problem with this part of the class as a whole. I also realize this could just be me, and my review should be taken with at least a grain of salt due to my meager performance compared to the rest of the class. I didn't mention this before, but each exam was 15%, and there was no final exam. Regarding GeekOS, the TA's, especially Leo, really carried here. They were really helpful in getting some of the projects working, and I really wouldn't have passed the class without them. Though, I'd maybe argue they were a bit too necessary to get through the projects. It's very clear the project specs haven't been updated in years, and the project slides, especially for the later projects such as 4b and all of 5, don't seem at all sufficient in getting you through the projects. Of course, the projects should be challenging, but in my experience, there was a lot of frustration due to how much information the slides and specs omit. For example, in project 5, file systems, GFS3 is a completely proprietary file system, yet we're not really given a good specification of it. For example, we were only given one example GFS3 image whose structure is completely undocumented. In project 4b, demand paging (the hardest project imo, though I hated 5 more just by nature), the way in which we were basically required to do things isn't very easy to deduce from source code, and the slides honestly made it more confusing what we had to do. Don't get me wrong, these projects are pretty cool at the end of the day, and honestly it was very useful being forced to navigate and implement significant components into a Linux-like kernel. I just think the projects would be better if the provided resources were more helpful. Finally, there's grading. The class is graded on a curve. This semester, seemingly a lot of insanely smart people took the class, which seemingly skewed the grade distribution like crazy. There was a review last semester of someone getting an 88 with Dr. Agrawala and ending with an A+. I know someone who got like an 89 this semester and ended with an A-. Take that for what you will. Overall, I can't say I don't recommend taking this class at all, but I have some issues with it. Pete is teaching this class next spring, so it seems for a little bit, Dr. Agrawala and Pete are alternating teaching this class.

review_text: I'd give 4.7 stars if PlanetTerp had such an option. This is a hard class. Not in the way that MATH140/141 are considered "hard", or in the way that Kruskal's classes are "hard" (at least his 351), but rather it is hard by virtue of the material. Algorithms are just often difficult concepts to grasp and really understand to the depth that Childs' wants his students to be able to grasp and understand for his assignments and exams. The class is paced quite nicely for me - I showed up to every lecture, and I feel like I gained something from each one. I was able to ask questions pretty frequently (perhaps too frequently), and Childs' would always spend the time to think about an answer to each one, and I felt that that helped me understand the material greatly. He records all of his lectures and posts all of his notes. The only things from class not available asynchronously online are the Q&A times that he holds in the 5-10 minutes before each class begins. The assignments are hard. (Did I mention the class is hard?) The first two took me about 10 hours each, and the other three 15-20 hours each. Each one is a set of five problems, the answers to which require (unless you're a super-mega-genius I guess) intuition and material from the lectures. A quote from one of his office hours: "If you're stuck on this problem, think about the algorithms we covered in class; I make the homeworks directly related [to those]." - Childs My strategy for the homeworks were to look at the problems when they were assigned, then keep them in mind over the next two weeks of lectures (each assignment is assigned exactly two weeks before they're due). Spending the time to actually understand the material on them is definitely helpful - they're actually harder than the exam questions by a solid margin, and they mirror the exam structure. Also, he drops the lowest of the five assignments, so each of your best four assignments comprise 10% of your final grade. Considering that there is ample time for each one, it's definitely possible to have the assignments be the grade fallback. The exams are hard. (yes.) The midterm is worth 20% of your final grade, and the final 40%. There's definitely a time-crunch aspect to this. As of writing this review, I haven't taken the final yet. But speaking from the midterm experience, there wasn't a single student that left the exam room early (shocker). Although it seemed like most of the class felt pretty bad about the midterm, to Childs', the midterm was "on the easier side." (Avg 69, median 70 iirc) I did well enough not to have major complaints about it, and other reviews go more in-depth. The textbook is... something that I didn't read. I'm sure it was useful to those who did, but the lectures + questions + office hours + assignments prepared me well enough to face the exams. Although Childs' is a great lecturer and all-around smart guy, he's definitely a bit hard to talk to. He feels like a classic computer-focused guy (which is fair, since he's getting paid for it lol), and I definitely agree with the previous reviewer that said it felt impossible to build rapport with him. TL;DR: Great lecturer, fair class, hard af so look at the grade distr. to make your choice
evidence_snippet: other three 15-20 hours each
label_rationale: Homework and exams are very difficult and time-intensive, but closely aligned with lectures and described as fair.

review_text: pedram, the goat that you are... to start off, I want to clarify a couple of things: 1. this was the summer version, so 15 weeks of content condensed to 10 weeks 2. all lectures were recorded bc of this, but there were virtual labs and q&a sessions 3. I never considered myself to be such a visual learner until I took this class. I appreciate that he takes the time to draw both the stack and the heap when explaining concepts such as recursion and the initialization of data structures. I found myself also drawing things out when I wanted to figure out the logic for my projects. he is really great at breaking things down and his slidesets are always very thorough and to the point. I also really liked that he included applications to the real world of what we are learning because it just makes what you're learning a lot cooler yk. projects: the projects that he assigned were somewhat challenging but not to the point where they were impossible. i'd recommend that you just sit with a problem for a while because the answer will come to you eventually if you give yourself enough time. I'm not gonna lie, I lowkey enjoyed them. the projects are pretty much free 100s as long as you submit on time and pass all tests. the content from the projects will basically be most related to what he will test you on the exams, so it's important that you don't chatgpt your way through them. quizzes: idk if this is the case for fall & spring semesters, but our quizzes were not weighted very much and were open note save for the debug quiz (lowkey kinda a joke but appreciated). make sure you do well on them because they're a way to get some easy points. exams: something that pedram does which is such a lifesaver is that he gives an outline of the exam two days prior to it. it contains the methods you will need to know for the exams, what the exam will and will not cover, and how many questions/what type of questions will be present. HYPERFOCUS ON THIS. you don't want to end up spending all your time studying something that won't even be covered. the previous year exams that he gives are good practice, but don't rely entirely on them. simply do the problems related to what the exams will test you on. the exams themselves were pretty fair. since this was a summer class, we had 1 hour and 20 min long exams for the first two exams and then 2 hours for the final. however, our exams were longer since we had more time. for the first time in a cs class ever, I was able to finish an exam in the allotted time for all 3 exams which was a win. I think maybe pedram has changed, but the exams seemed reasonable to complete in the time that he provided. I gotta say that I am not the fastest in terms of algorithmic thinking, but I still felt that I had enough time to complete the coding questions on time. exam structure was generally multiple choice & short answer that tested you on theory, sorting algs (if applicable), and other coding-adjacent concepts like logs and whatnot. the coding questions never require more than 10-15 lines of code to properly fulfill all the requirements for the method. some examples of code-writing questions are completing methods for a class or using data structures to perform certain tasks. all were pretty doable and I'm glad that he tests us on thinking algorithmically bc that's a skill you need as a computer scientist. tips & tricks: - start projects early, but you alr knew that (genuinely it's the best way to actually master concepts from lecture) - also figure out the logic for your projects before your fingers touch the keyboard (will save you lots of strife) - listen to lectures on 2x speed - go over content from exam guidelines religiously - if you lowkey didn't understand anything fom 131 make sure you fully understand the content (I used Alex Lee/Bro Code which I found pretty helpful) - this might be a me thing but don't overtake notes, simply go back to the slides or rewatch lectures as necessary (I found that taking excessive notes were kind of a waste of time) - GO TO DISCUSSION or at least catch up on them immediately if you can't make it since they are essentially mini lectures that cover high-yield content that WILL be tested on exams (ex: sorting algs were taught during discussion which showed up in pretty much every exam) shout out to the TAs! angie, ryan, and brian have saved my life on more than one occassion! this was a pretty memorable class and it's safe to say I feel more confident to take on cs now 😎

review_text: He is an alright instructor. At the beginning of the semester, I had issues with his policies regarding technology in his class, since I primarily take notes on my laptop, and he only allows pencil and paper for notes in his class. Along with that, he does have a weird beef with smartphones, strictly banning them from his class. While these issues are really annoying, I can understand why he has them in place; it keeps students focused on the content he is teaching, and you retain more information when you write stuff down on paper. Now for the actual gripes I have with him that caused him to lose two stars, since he has that ban on cellphones, he also tells people to put them away when he sees someone using a phone, but he ends up wasting at the very least 5 minutes of class time just saying "Hey can you put away your phone" or "Hey can you take out your ear buds, no electronic devices". Regarding the actual lectures, they are really boring, but I wouldn't expect anything else from a computer science lecture. The pace of the lecture is quite fast, and if you are not a fast writer (like me), then you are in a bit of trouble, and most of your notes will end up looking like chicken scratch. The content can be a little challenging, but honestly, I've found that this class is slightly easier than CMSC131 (but that is because the instructor for that class was one of the absolute worst ones I've ever had in my life). For the first month or so of class it will drag on if you take this class right after CMSC131 due to the fact that a good amount of the lectures at the beginning of the class just recap old CMSC131, but I wouldn't get too comfortable with that since it does quickly move onto new content that you will need for the exams and projects. While on the topic of the exams, they are absolutely some of the most difficult exams I've taken in college. I have plenty of gripes with his exams, the first of these is that for the multiple-choice section of the exams, he will take points off if you select the wrong answer instead of the question just not giving credit. Because of this grading policy, I've had one of his exams go from a high D (still a low grade, I know) to a high E. Along with that, the content on these exams is very difficult, from the coding questions to the multiple choice questions, after you leave the exam room, it will have you wondering if you even studied for it. Also, on some occasions, the practice exams that he gives are nothing like the actual exam, so if you use the practice exam to study and he decides to change up the format, then you are doomed. Onto some of the positives of Herman's class, he does try to break up the monotony of his class by joking around with the students and just throwing a couple of jokes here and there to break it up. Also, he uses the students sitting in the front row to use as examples for how different concepts work, which ends up being a lot more informative than him just talking and talking about it with some slides on the screen. The lecture slides are not the most informative, so while he does say that you can always view the slides after the class if you miss something, you can't really since you won't have him explaining some of the concepts that he left off of the lecture slides. The projects that he gives, while there are a lot of them and most of the time they are pretty hard, have guidelines that are extremely informative and can actually guide the code design if you reread it when you don't really know what to do. Overall, Larry Herman is an alright instructor (if you take this class do not call him professor) with some odd policies that make sense when yuo really think about them, but he also has a fair share of negatives to consider before registering for his class. Grade: 6.5/10, Not the first choice class, but not the last choice

The professors put in the bare minimum effort, more or less entirely ripping off Berkeley's CS188 course (https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/fa23/), including all of the topics and slides. Moving on to the quality of the lectures, Dr. Kim seems very knowledgeable, but she simply cannot teach effectively and seems best suited for research. Her lectures pretty much consisted of reading off the Berkeley slides and giving inadequate answers when anyone would ask a question. It seems that there was very minimal preparation done before the lectures. I personally learned more putting in headphones and reading the Berkeley notes instead of listening to her. The assignments didn't make the course any better either… There was one midterm exam, which was a disaster. The professors made us take the exam on Gradescope on our laptops in class, because their goal was not to measure students' comprehension of the material but instead to minimize the time and effort needed to grade the exam while maintaining the façade of a well-run class. They provided hardly any review materials themselves and only posted full solutions after complaints on Piazza. And even the solutions provided turned out to have errors. Besides that, they pointed us to Berkeley's past exams, which ended up being nothing like our exam. The exam was such a time crunch that hardly anyone could even finish, and they had to curve the exam to be out of 78 points even though there were well over 100 points originally. The first 2 homework assignments were quite boring, but Homework 3 (a PyTorch lab which involved building an image classifier from scratch) turned out to be quite interesting. However, the professors did not teach us anything to equip us with the knowledge necessary to do the homework. They did not go over how to use PyTorch, how to design a neural network, how convolutional neural networks work, how to improve models, or anything else that would be remotely useful. While this was one of the only thought-provoking assignments, the professors did not prepare us for it at all. Finally, we had a group project due at the end of the semester that was pretty interesting, but the professors did not communicate the requirements clearly at all. They waited until a week before the end of the semester to tell us the details of the final poster presentation and announce that we had to complete a 3-5 page report in addition to the deliverables that we proposed in our project proposals. Somehow, the poster presentation was worth 70%, while the rest of the deliverables combined (including the 3-5 page report and all of the code) were worth just 30%. Overall, it seems like not much thought was put in this course. Why am I paying for a cheap rip-off of a Berkeley course that is freely available to all?

review_text: Very organized. Set up Piazza and office hours times weeks before the semester began. He knows the textbook forwards and backwards. He follows the assigned textbook readings very closely. So if you're struggling to keep up during lecture, do the assigned readings beforehand. The homework are long. HW3 (dynamic programming) was especially difficult. Make sure to start early (you're given 2 weeks to complete). The consist of 5 questions, typically all questions (except the NP HW) ask you to write an algorithm, prove its correctness, and state its running time. Use the textbook to complete homework early. Do not start any later than a week before the deadline. Each assignment took 10-20 hours to complete. Make sure to go to office hours to verify your thought process or you may get half credit on questions you incorrectly approach. The homework is however very fair and directly relevant to what we covered in class. HW average between 80-90%. I think what made me respect Prof Childs the most was that he was willing to answer questions during lectures fully. Even if this meant we did not get through supplementary topics at the end of the semester (had to cut out quantum lecture but posted for viewing on ELMS), he made sure to take any question serious and answer it without making anyone feel stupid. That's a classroom culture I appreciate. Sometimes however he does rush at the end to finish a proof if we got derailed with too many questions, but usually he saves it for the next class. During office hours, he was helpful. He gave hints on how to approach the homework. It was honestly helpful to explain my thought process and get that feedback from him. He allows multiple students in Zoom room at once or in person, so you get to listen to other students questions and perspectives as well, which is enriching. In regards to what 2 reviews down said about rapport, I will say that my interactions during office hours were mostly focused on course material and homework or practice problems. I think it is possible to build rapport, but you'll have to come with questions and willingness to share your interests. Most importantly, I felt like he did care about me and my understanding of the material. Sometimes he cracks jokes. Regarding exams, he made an especially difficult/ time crunch midterm (60% average), but he adjusted for it with a more lenient final exam (75% average). Overall cutoffs for the course: A-: 84, B-: 71, C-: 58. The biggest advice for exams I can give is to understand the homework well (what are the key concepts, thought processes), but then make sure to do as many practice problems as possible. Get your thought process verified by Childs or a TA. Big shout out to Aditya Acharya. He is the best TA for the course, go to his office hours if you can!! He makes his office hours basically into a discussion section for the course, white boarding concepts and helping get started on homework. Advice: Start HW early (1+ week) so that you can spend 10-20 hours. Stay up to date with the lecture. Attend in person if you can even though its recorded. Take advantage of Piazza since Childs responds very actively. Take advantage of office hours, especially TA OH for homework. Prepare early for the exams. Good luck! Take him if you have the privilege and get a seat. I feel like I learned a lot and it greatly helped me with my logical/algorithmic thinking.
